accepted.question_text: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, starting from a smooth divergence-free initial velocity field, what are the most general assumptions on that initial field that guarantee the existence of a smooth solution for all times t greater than or equal to 0 rather than the formation of a finite-time singularity? The same question is also asked for the Euler equations.
accepted.context_brief: Global regularity from smooth initial data

evidence.quote: Question 3.1. What are the most general conditions for smooth initial incompressible velocity field ~v(~x, 0) that ensures that smooth solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations exist for t ≥ 0? The same question holds for Euler’s equations.

Then, question 3.1 is related to the problem of whether the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations can develop a finite time singularity from these smooth initial conditions or if a (unique) global smooth solution exists, which means smooth for all times.

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism could generate finite-time blow-up for solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations when the initial velocity field is smooth and incompressible? In particular, can one understand physically how singular behavior would arise from such smooth initial data rather than from pathological initial conditions?

evidence.quote: Question 3.2. Can we understand physically the mechanism that could generate finite time blow-up of solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations starting from smooth initial incompressible velocity field?
This discussion suggests that the study of the physical vortex dynamics (for itself), specifically local vortex stretching mechanisms, could be an interesting approach to the Millennium problem.

accepted.question_text: Which properties of the velocity field are sufficient to guarantee the existence of a unique global smooth solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for all times, assuming the initial conditions are already smooth? This asks for structural conditions on the evolving velocity field that rule out singularity formation and ensure global regularity.

evidence.quote: Question 3.3. Following the previous questions, which properties of the velocity field would be needed to guarantee the existence of a (unique) global smooth solution at all times, once the initial conditions are smooth?
Unfortunately, there is no way to prove that the L4(IR3) norm of the velocity field is bounded at all times based solely on Navier-Stokes equations.

accepted.question_text: In relativistic heavy-ion collisions, can the pre-hydrodynamic stage create the condition needed for relativistic hydrodynamics to apply at the later hydrodynamic stage, namely local thermodynamic equilibrium in which the mean free path λmfp of the elementary constituents is much smaller than a characteristic system size L? Equivalently, can step (i) of the collision dynamics produce a medium that satisfies λmfp much less than L by the time step (ii) begins?

evidence.quote: Question 4.1. We know from section 2 that applicability of hydrodynamics relies on the existence of a local thermodynamic equilibrium and thus on the condition that the mean free path of elementary constituents λmf p is much smaller than a dimension scale of the system under consideration L. Can step (i) create this condition that could prevail at step (ii)?
The question is then whether their interactions are frequent enough for thermodynamic equilibrium to be established.

accepted.question_text: How can one define the most plausible initial conditions at the beginning of the hydrodynamic stage in a relativistic heavy-ion collision? The issue is to specify the initial relativistic-fluid state at the start of stage (ii), even though the experimentally observed hadrons are produced only much later and the earlier state cannot be measured directly.

evidence.quote: Question 4.2. How can we define the most plausible initial conditions at the beginning of step (ii)?
The problem linked to initial conditions is that this is very unclear how to specify these conditions in the experimental context described here.

accepted.question_text: To what extent do the experimental observables measured after hadron formation in relativistic heavy-ion collisions mainly reflect the geometry of the collision, and how can that collision geometry be inferred from those final-state hadronic observables? This question concerns the part of the initial conditions that is tied to the geometry of the collision and how that geometric information survives through hydrodynamic expansion and decoupling.
accepted.context_brief: Recovering collision geometry from final observables

evidence.quote: Question 4.3. Clearly, these initial conditions will contain the physics of the state of matter created during the collision, through the equation of state. This is where the physics comes in. Then, the coupling of the equation of state and the equations of fluid mechanics will govern the expansion of matter at stage (ii) up to (iii). However, this program can only be achieved with another essential part of the initial conditions related to the geometry of the collision. How this geometry can be inferred at step (iii) once the observed hadrons are formed. The immediate question that follows is whether the experimental observables does depend mainly on the geometry of the collision or not.
A complete set of initial conditions involves the three component of the velocity field, the energy and entropy density, at each point in space and at time t0.

accepted.question_text: How can one explicitly construct solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations that either blow up in finite time or remain globally regular, so that the possibility of finite-time singularity formation from smooth initial data can be tested directly rather than only indirectly through a priori estimates?

evidence.quote: How can we build explicitly blowing up or not solutions of Navier-Stokes equations?

Conjecture 5.3. From the discussion of questions 3.1 and 3.2, we can think that a solution to the Millennium problem would be to show that it is always possible to construct mathematically a solution that diverges in a finite time, following the cascade behavior (above), apart from some specific initial conditions like small initial data where the global regularity is ensured.
